title: Juwayriyyah's freed people
hook: a captive comes to ask for help with her freedom, and her marriage sets her people free (Abu Dawud)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zaynab bint Khuzaymah, whose story survives as a name. Your line was: mother of the poor. Did a meal go to someone who couldn't repay you? Day eight hundred fourteen.

A battle is over, and the losing tribe's people are captives. Among them is the daughter of their chief. She has made an agreement to buy her own freedom, and she can't pay it. So she does something brave: she goes straight to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, to ask for help. Aisha, watching her come to the door, tells us in Abu Dawud's collection what happened next. Today: Juwayriyyah's freed people.
screen: `A CHIEF'S DAUGHTER, CAPTIVE.` → `SHE CAN'T PAY FOR HER FREEDOM.` → `SHE GOES TO ASK.`

segments.voice: The tribe was the Banu al-Mustaliq, and the woman was Juwayriyyah, daughter of their chief, al-Harith. In the report, she tells the Prophet plainly who she is, what has happened to her, and that she needs help paying for her freedom. He offers her something better: he will pay what she owes and marry her. She accepts. Then comes the part the story is really about. The news goes around the camp: the Prophet has married Juwayriyyah. And the companions, who were holding her people as captives, said, in effect: these are now the Prophet's in-laws. How can we keep his relatives as captives? And they let them go. The report counts it: through that marriage, a hundred households of the Banu al-Mustaliq were set free. Then Aisha adds a sentence of her own. She says she knew of no woman who was a greater blessing to her people than Juwayriyyah. One woman walked in to ask about her own freedom. Her people walked out free. Look at the chain. Her courage to ask. His answer, larger than the question. And then the companions, who weren't commanded to do anything, choosing on their own to free people because of a new family tie. Honor for one person spread outward until it became freedom for many. One more glimpse: Sahih Muslim has Juwayriyyah sitting in her place of prayer from dawn until the late morning, remembering Allah. The woman who brought freedom to a whole tribe is remembered at prayer, too. A blessing to her people.
screen: `SHE TELLS HIM WHO SHE IS.` · `HE PAYS AND MARRIES HER.` · `HOW CAN WE HOLD HIS IN-LAWS?` · `A HUNDRED HOUSEHOLDS FREED.` · then, large: `A BLESSING TO HER PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: The practice: free someone from a burden. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone near you carrying something they can't put down on their own. A chore that's swallowing them, an apology they're waiting for, a grudge you're holding against them, a worry nobody has helped with. Which of those could you lift? Not everything. One thing. See yourself lifting it: doing the task, saying the word, letting the grudge go, sitting with the worry. If you pray, you can ask to be a blessing to the people around you. The bell holds the time.
Juwayriyyah, the chief's daughter who asked the Prophet for help with her freedom, and whose marriage led the companions to free a hundred households. Today's word.
Your line: a blessing to her people. Today, lift one burden off one person, and let it spread. Day eight hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Muslims honor Juwayriyyah bint al-Harith among the mothers of the believers, retelling from Sunan Abi Dawud how her marriage led to the freeing of her people, and many learn the words of remembrance taught to her in Sahih Muslim.

fork.setup: you are a companion holding captives from her tribe. you hear the Prophet has just married Juwayriyyah. what do you do?
options: keep them; nothing has been commanded.
free them, since they're now his in-laws.
ask the Prophet what he wants done.
fork.reveal: the report says they freed them, saying the Prophet's in-laws should not be held captive.

trapdoor: what you thought: a marriage in a list of marriages.
what it means: one woman's courage and one marriage led to the freedom of her people.
what a scholar hears: Sunan Abi Dawud 3931 for the story and Aisha's words; Sahih Muslim 2726 for Juwayriyyah at prayer from dawn to late morning.
